meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to mean'.

examples.trans: Pasha, what does all this mean?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что? Ты мне ухо отрежешь?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what? Will you cut my ear off?

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мысл'). Common masculine noun meaning 'sense, meaning' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What do you mean? Where is Mishkin?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'devil, darn' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Чёрт, я запутался. Это опасная идея.
examples.trans: Darn, I am confused. This is a dangerous idea.
What on earth kind of acclimatization?!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'путаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'get confused, get tangled', paired with 'запутываться'.

examples.text: Я совсем запутался в этих правилах.
examples.trans: I got completely confused by these rules.

examples.text: Чёрт, я запутался. Это опасная идея.
examples.trans: Darn, I am confused. This is a dangerous idea.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no; there isn't', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'no ... at all, not any', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I have no money at all.

examples.text: Да нет у тебя никаких денег.
examples.trans: But you don't have any money.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'so that, in order to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to leave, go away', paired with 'уходить'.
Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'ождать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'wait', paired with 'ждать'.

examples.text: Подожди, Нин, ты не поняла. Это же стыдно!
examples.trans: Wait, Nina, you don't get it. It's shameful!
Wait, where are you two going?

examples.text: Подождите! Два дня — это же очень мало.
examples.trans: Hold on! Two days is far too little.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to leave, to go away', paired with 'уйти'.
High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'if', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to say, to tell', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ерьёзно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
